title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Event Stores
summary: An event store is an append-only, immutable, time-ordered log of domain events where each event represents a state transition that has already happened (past tense, business-meaningful), forming the foundation of event…
objectives: What is the difference between event sourcing and a traditional CRUD database?
How does optimistic concurrency work in an event store, and why is it preferred over pessimistic locking?
What is a snapshot, and how does it solve the "replay performance" problem?
Explain the difference between an event store and a message broker like Kafka/RabbitMQ.

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** An **event store** is an *append-only, immutable, time-ordered log of domain events* where each event represents a state transition that has already happened (past tense, business-meaningful), forming the foundation of **event sourcing** — instead of storing current state, you store the sequence of events that led to that state, and reconstruct state by replaying — exemplified by **EventStoreDB** (purpose-built), **Apache Kafka** (event-log-as-database pattern), **Apache Pulsar**, and **AWS Kinesis**, with **snapshots** for fast reads and **projections** for queryable read models.

Traditional databases store current state: a `users` table has a row `alice, email=alice@x.com, plan=pro`. When Alice upgrades from free to pro, you `UPDATE users SET plan='pro' WHERE id=alice` — and the historical fact "Alice was on free plan from Jan to March, then upgraded to pro" is lost (unless you maintain a separate audit log). **Event sourcing** inverts this: the database stores the *events* (`UserCreated`, `PlanChanged`), and current state is derived by replaying them. The event store is the system of record; the "current state" is a projection. This pattern gives you perfect auditability (every state change is recorded), time travel (replay events up to timestamp T to see state at T), and decoupling (multiple read models can be built from the same event stream). The trade-off is complexity: you must design events carefully, handle event schema evolution, build idempotent consumers, and manage eventual consistency between the event log and read models. The pattern is increasingly popular for financial systems (every transaction must be auditable), collaborative apps (Google Docs-style conflict resolution), and microservices (event log as the integration layer).

The fundamental data structure of an event store is an **append-only log** — events are written once, never modified, never deleted (with rare exceptions like GDPR right-to-be-forgotten which requires special handling). Each event has: an *event ID* (UUID), a *stream ID* (logical grouping, e.g., `user-42` for all events about user 42), an *event type* (`UserCreated`, `PlanChanged`), a *sequence number* (monotonic per stream, used for optimistic concurrency), a *timestamp*, and a *payload* (JSON or protobuf). Appends are O(1) sequential writes; reads are range scans by stream ID and sequence number. **EventStoreDB** (formerly Event Store, .NET-based, open-source) is the canonical purpose-built event store — streams, optimistic concurrency via expected version numbers, subscriptions (catch-up, persistent, volatile), and built-in projections (JavaScript-based). **Apache Kafka** can be used as an event store via the "event log as database" pattern: each stream is a Kafka topic, each event is a message, and consumers maintain their own offsets; the log is retained for days/weeks/forever depending on configuration. **Apache Pulsar** adds tiered storage (hot/warm/cold) for indefinite retention. **AWS Kinesis Data Streams** is the managed equivalent with 365-day retention. The choice depends on ecosystem: Kafka dominates microservices, EventStoreDB is purpose-built for DDD/event-sourcing apps, Pulsar for multi-tenant scale.

The hard problem in event sourcing is **replay performance**. To answer "what is Alice's current state?", you must replay every event in stream `user-42` from sequence 1 to N. For a stream with 10,000 events, this is slow on every read. **Snapshots** solve this: periodically (every 100 events, or when state size exceeds a threshold), persist the current aggregate state as a snapshot. On read, load the latest snapshot and replay only events after it. If a snapshot exists at sequence 9500, you load it and replay events 9501-10000 — 50 events instead of 10000. Snapshots are an optimization, not part of the source of truth; if they're lost or corrupted, the event log still has everything and you can rebuild. The trade-off: snapshot schema must evolve with the aggregate schema (if you change the `User` aggregate, old snapshots may be incompatible). Mitigation: version the snapshot schema, or rebuild snapshots from scratch on schema change. **Projections** solve a different problem: the event log is optimized for appends, not queries. "Find all users on the pro plan" requires scanning every stream. A projection is a derived read model built by subscribing to the event log and updating a query-optimized store (PostgreSQL table, Redis hash, Elasticsearch index). When a `PlanChanged` event arrives, the projection updates a `users_by_plan` table. Projections are eventually consistent (lag of milliseconds to seconds) and can be rebuilt from the event log at any time.

Real-world deployments illustrate the pattern. **Netflix's billing system** uses event sourcing — every billing event (subscription start, upgrade, payment, refund) is appended to an event stream, and the current account state is derived. This gives perfect auditability for financial compliance, the ability to replay events to diagnose disputes, and decoupling between the billing engine (writes events) and the invoicing/notification services (consume events). **LinkedIn uses Kafka** as the central nervous system — every profile view, connection, message, and job application is an event in Kafka, consumed by dozens of downstream services (recommendation, analytics, notifications, search indexing). Kafka at LinkedIn processes trillions of events per day across thousands of topics. **Uber's billing and trip lifecycle** are event-sourced — every trip state change (requested, accepted, started, completed, paid) is an event, enabling accurate fare disputes and analytics. **Amazon's shopping cart and order lifecycle** are event-sourced internally (the DynamoDB Streams + Lambda pattern is essentially event sourcing on AWS managed services). **Wise (TransferWise)** publicly discusses using event sourcing for cross-border money transfers — every step (transfer initiated, funds received, currency converted, payout sent) is an event, auditable end-to-end. The common thread: when business correctness requires a perfect audit trail, when multiple services need to react to the same business events, or when you need time-travel debugging, event sourcing is the answer.

The trade-offs explain why event sourcing isn't the default architecture. First, **cognitive complexity** — developers must think in terms of events, not CRUD; a simple "update user email" becomes "emit `EmailChanged` event, apply it to the aggregate, project to the read model." The mental model shift is significant. Second, **event schema evolution** — events are immutable, but schemas evolve. Adding a field is easy (default value), but renaming or removing a field requires upcasting (transforming old events on read) or versioned events. Tools like EventStoreDB's upcasters and Kafka's Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf with backward compatibility) help. Third, **eventual consistency** — the read model lags behind the event log by milliseconds to seconds; users may see stale data immediately after a write. UI patterns (optimistic UI, "saving..." indicators) help. Fourth, **system complexity** — you now have an event store, a snapshot store, multiple projections, and consumers; more moving parts to monitor and operate. Fifth, **debugging is harder** — to reproduce a bug, you may need to replay a specific stream's events through a specific version of the aggregate. Sixth, **deletes are awkward** — GDPR's right-to-be-forgotten requires either encrypting events with per-user keys (and deleting the key) or rewriting the log to remove PII. Seventh, **transactional boundaries** — a single event append is atomic, but multi-stream transactions are not (you need sagas or process managers). The takeaway: event sourcing is a powerful pattern for audit-heavy, integration-heavy domains, but it adds real complexity. Use it when the business value (auditability, time-travel, decoupling) outweighs the operational cost.

(send upgrade email)"] C2["Analytics service
(track conversion)"] C3["Audit log
(compliance)"] end LOG --> C1 LOG --> C2 LOG --> C3 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Event sourcing: store events, derive state Traditional CRUD: Event sourcing: +-----------------+ +--------------------------+ | users | | Event Log (immutable): | | id | email |plan| | stream user-42: | | 42 | a@x | pro | <- current | E1 UserCreated | +-----------------+ | E2 EmailSet(a@x) | UPDATE loses history | E3 PlanChanged(free) | | E4 ... | | E6 PlanChanged(pro) | +--------------------------+ | | replay v +--------------------------+ | User aggregate state: | | email=a@x, plan=pro | +--------------------------+ Event store = append-only log of (stream, version, type, payload, ts) +----------+-------+-----------------+----------------+-------+ | stream | ver | event_type | payload | ts | +----------+-------+-----------------+----------------+-------+ | user-42 | 1 | UserCreated | {name:'Alice'} | t1 | | user-42 | 2 | EmailSet | {email:'a@x'} | t2 | | user-42 | 3 | PlanChanged | {plan:'free'} | t3 | | user-42 | 4 | PlanChanged | {plan:'pro'} | t4 | <-- append-only | user-99 | 1 | UserCreated | {name:'Bob'} | t5 | (no UPDATE, no DELETE) +----------+-------+-----------------+----------------+-------+ Snapshots: persist aggregate state every N events to speed up reads user-42 @ v4: {email:'a@x', plan:'pro'} <-- snapshot Read user-42: load snapshot v4, replay E5..EN (not E1..EN) Projections: build query-optimized read models from event log Event Log -> [Projection] -> users_by_plan table (PostgreSQL) | -> search_index (Elasticsearch) | -> notification_queue (Kafka) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A command arrives at the application: `ChangePlan(user_id=42, new_plan='pro')`. The application loads the User aggregate by reading stream `user-42` from the event store. To optimize, it first checks the snapshot store for the latest snapshot (say, version 4), loads that, then replays only events 5..N from the event log to get current state. The aggregate validates the command (e.g., "user must be active," "plan must be valid") and emits a domain event `PlanChanged(plan='pro')`. 2. The event is appended to stream `user-42` with `expected_version=N` (optimistic concurrency: if another writer appended to the same stream between load and append, the version mismatch causes a `WrongExpectedVersion` exception, and the command is retried). The append is atomic and durable (fsynced to disk, replicated). After append, the application can either return success to the client immediately (the event is committed) or wait for the projection to update (stronger consistency, slower). 3. Projections and consumers subscribe to the event log. A catch-up subscription reads new events as they arrive; a persistent subscription tracks consumer offsets and supports competing consumers. The `users_by_plan` projection receives `PlanChanged`, updates the PostgreSQL table `users_by_plan` (decrement free count, increment pro count). The notification service sends Alice an upgrade confirmation email. The analytics service tracks conversion funnels. All consumers are decoupled — adding a new consumer doesn't affect existing ones. Real-world: Netflix's billing emits events consumed by invoicing, tax calculation, fraud detection, and analytics services — all decoupled via the event log.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Append-only event store with snapshots and projections.
- An immutable domain event.
- Append-only log of events, grouped by stream.
- Append events to a stream with optimistic concurrency check.
- Commands (return events to append)
- We need prior plan; in real systems, projection tracks per-user state
- Here we assume upgrade from "free" (simplified)
- Load aggregate (replays events)

**Defines:** `Event`, `EventStore`, `UserAggregate`, `UsersByPlanProjection`

```python
"""
Append-only event store with snapshots and projections.

Demonstrates:
  - Streams (per-aggregate event sequences)
  - Optimistic concurrency (expected_version)
  - Snapshots (persist aggregate state every N events)
  - Projections (build read models from event stream)
  - Replay (reconstruct state from event log)

Models EventStoreDB-style event sourcing.

Run:  python3 event_store.py
"""

import json
import time
import uuid
from collections import defaultdict

class Event:
    """An immutable domain event."""

    def __init__(self, stream_id, version, event_type, payload, timestamp=None):
        self.event_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
        self.stream_id = stream_id
        self.version = version            # monotonic per-stream
        self.event_type = event_type
        self.payload = payload
        self.timestamp = timestamp or time.time()

    def to_dict(self):
        return {"event_id": self.event_id, "stream_id": self.stream_id,
                "version": self.version, "event_type": self.event_type,
                "payload": self.payload, "timestamp": self.timestamp}

class EventStore:
    """Append-only log of events, grouped by stream."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._streams = defaultdict(list)   # stream_id -> [Event]
        self._snapshots = {}                # stream_id -> (version, state)

    def append(self, stream_id, events, expected_version=None):
        """Append events to a stream with optimistic concurrency check."""
        current = len(self._streams[stream_id])
        if expected_version is not None and expected_version != current:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"WrongExpectedVersion: stream={stream_id} "
                f"expected={expected_version} actual={current}"
            )
        for ev in events:
            current += 1
            ev.stream_id = stream_id
            ev.version = current
            self._streams[stream_id].append(ev)

    def read_stream(self, stream_id, from_version=0):
        return [e for e in self._streams[stream_id] if e.version > from_version]

    # ----- snapshots -----
    def save_snapshot(self, stream_id, version, state):
        self._snapshots[stream_id] = (version, state)

    def load_snapshot(self, stream_id):
        return self._snapshots.get(stream_id)

class UserAggregate:
    """Replays events to build current state. Emits new events on commands."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.id = None
        self.email = None
        self.plan = "free"
        self.version = 0

    def apply(self, event):
        """Fold an event into state (pure state transition)."""
        if event.event_type == "UserCreated":
            self.id = event.payload["user_id"]
        elif event.event_type == "EmailSet":
            self.email = event.payload["email"]
        elif event.event_type == "PlanChanged":
            self.plan = event.payload["plan"]
        self.version = event.version

    @classmethod
    def from_events(cls, store, stream_id):
        """Replay events (use snapshot if available) to rebuild state."""
        agg = cls()
        snap = store.load_snapshot(stream_id)
        from_v = 0
        if snap:
            agg.id = snap[1].get("id")
            agg.email = snap[1].get("email")
            agg.plan = snap[1].get("plan", "free")
            agg.version = snap[0]
            from_v = snap[0]
        for event in store.read_stream(stream_id, from_version=from_v):
            agg.apply(event)
        return agg

    # ----- commands (return events to append) -----
    @staticmethod
    def create(user_id, email):
        return [Event(None, 0, "UserCreated", {"user_id": user_id}),
                Event(None, 0, "EmailSet", {"email": email})]

    @staticmethod
    def change_plan(new_plan):
        if new_plan not in ("free", "pro", "enterprise"):
            raise ValueError(f"invalid plan: {new_plan}")
        return [Event(None, 0, "PlanChanged", {"plan": new_plan})]

class UsersByPlanProjection:
    """Subscribes to event log, maintains a read model: plan -> user count."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.counts = defaultdict(int)

    def handle(self, event):
        if event.event_type == "UserCreated":
            self.counts["free"] += 1
        elif event.event_type == "PlanChanged":
            # We need prior plan; in real systems, projection tracks per-user state
            # Here we assume upgrade from "free" (simplified)
            if event.payload["plan"] != "free":
                self.counts["free"] = max(0, self.counts["free"] - 1)
                self.counts[event.payload["plan"]] += 1

# ---------------- demo ----------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    store = EventStore()
    projection = UsersByPlanProjection()

    print("=== Create user alice (stream user-42) ===")
    events = UserAggregate.create(42, "alice@example.com")
    store.append("user-42", events, expected_version=0)
    for ev in events:
        projection.handle(ev)
        print(f"  appended: {ev.event_type} {ev.payload} (v{ev.version})")

    print("\n=== Change alice's plan to 'pro' ===")
    # Load aggregate (replays events)
    alice = UserAggregate.from_events(store, "user-42")
    print(f"  current state: email={alice.email} plan={alice.plan} v{alice.version}")
    # Emit change event with optimistic concurrency
    new_events = alice.change_plan("pro")
    store.append("user-42", new_events, expected_version=alice.version)
    for ev in new_events:
        projection.handle(ev)
        print(f"  appended: {ev.event_type} {ev.payload} (v{ev.version})")

    print("\n=== Save snapshot at v3 ===")
    store.save_snapshot("user-42", 3, {"id": 42, "email": "alice@example.com",
                                       "plan": "pro"})

    print("\n=== Concurrent write attempt (expected_version mismatch) ===")
    try:
        bad_events = alice.change_plan("enterprise")  # stale alice (doesn't know v3)
        store.append("user-42", bad_events, expected_version=alice.version)
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"  CONFLICT (expected): {e}")

    print("\n=== Reload aggregate (uses snapshot v3 + replays) ===")
    alice2 = UserAggregate.from_events(store, "user-42")
    print(f"  state: email={alice2.email} plan={alice2.plan} v{alice2.version}")

    print("\n=== Projection: users_by_plan ===")
    for plan, count in sorted(projection.counts.items()):
        print(f"  {plan}: {count}")

    print("\n=== Event log (immutable audit trail) ===")
    for ev in store.read_stream("user-42"):
        print(f"  v{ev.version} {ev.event_type} {ev.payload}  @ ts={ev.timestamp:.2f}")

    print("\n  Event-store trade-offs:")
    print("    + perfect audit trail (every state change recorded)")
    print("    + time travel (replay to any point in time)")
    print("    + decoupled consumers (projections, analytics, notifications)")
    print("    + optimistic concurrency (no locks)")
    print("    - complexity (events, projections, snapshots, schemas)")
    print("    - eventual consistency (read model lags event log)")
    print("    - schema evolution (upcasters, versioning)")
    print("    - deletes are awkward (GDPR right-to-be-forgotten)")
```
